glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: The chapter remembers Judah’s wider households and Simeon’s families and towns, and within these lists it pauses on Jabez, who called on the God of Israel and received what he asked.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: After David’s royal line in chapter 3, the record returns to Judah’s other families and then to Simeon, whose towns lay within Judah’s territory (Joshua 19:1–9).

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “And Jabez called on the God of Israel saying, ‘Oh, that You would bless me indeed, and enlarge my territory, that Your hand would be with me, and that You would keep me from evil, that I may not cause pain!’ So God granted him what he requested.” (1 Chronicles 4:10, NKJV)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
After the royal line of chapter 3, the record turns to ordinary households. Judah’s clans appear with their towns and their trades: craftsmen at Ge Harashim (4:14), linen workers (4:21), and potters who “dwelt with the king for his work” (4:23). Women are named as well, among them Bithiah “the daughter of Pharaoh” (4:18). God’s people included those who built, wove and shaped clay, as well as those who ruled.

In the middle of the list stands Jabez. His mother gave him a name that sounds like pain, saying, “Because I bore him in pain” (4:9), but Jabez “called on the God of Israel” (4:10). He asked for blessing, for enlarged territory, for God’s hand to be with him and for protection from evil, “that I may not cause pain” (4:10). The account ends simply: “So God granted him what he requested” (4:10). A name tied to pain did not decide his life, because he brought his need to the God of Israel.

The chapter then turns to Simeon, a smaller tribe whose families did not “multiply as much as the children of Judah” (4:27), and records its towns and later movements. The expedition to Gedor took place in Hezekiah’s reign; the expedition to Mount Seir is undated. From beginning to end the chapter shows a God who keeps the record of His people’s homes, work and prayers, and who hears those who call on Him.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
1 Chronicles 4:1–8 — Further Families of Judah

The genealogy returns to Judah’s families beyond the royal line, naming descendants of Shobal and Hur and the two wives of Ashhur the father of Tekoa. The names mix ancestors, clans and towns, tying families to the places they settled.

1 Chronicles 4:9–10 — The Prayer of Jabez

Jabez, more honorable than his brothers, calls on the God of Israel for blessing, enlarged territory, God’s hand with him, and protection from evil and pain. God grants his request, and the account adds no further details about his life.

1 Chronicles 4:11–23 — Clans, Craftsmen, and Potters of Judah

The record continues with Othniel, the sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh, Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, the house of the linen workers and the potters. These notes honor skilled and ordinary work, including service done for the king.

1 Chronicles 4:24–33 — Simeon’s Families and Towns

Simeon’s descendants are listed, with the note that their families did not grow like Judah’s. Their towns, including Beersheba and Ziklag, are named as their dwelling places until the reign of David.

1 Chronicles 4:34–43 — Simeon’s Expansion

Simeon’s leaders seek pasture for their flocks near Gedor, and in Hezekiah’s days they destroy the people living there and settle in their place. Five hundred Simeonites go to Mount Seir, defeat the remaining Amalekites and live there to the writer’s day.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Jabez’s prayer is one of the best-known passages in Chronicles, and the chapter shows why it matters: a person marked by pain can bring that need directly to God and ask for His blessing, His presence and His protection. Yet the passage reports one man’s request and God’s answer. It does not promise wealth, land or a painless life to everyone who repeats the words, and it should be read with the wider teaching of Scripture on asking according to God’s will (1 John 5:14).

The chapter also widens our sense of who counts in God’s story. Potters, linen workers, a smaller tribe and families looking for pasture all have a place in the record. Faithful prayer and honest work both belong to what one generation hands to the next.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Ordinary households remembered. Judah’s wider families and their towns stand alongside the royal line (4:1–8, 11–23).

Calling on the God of Israel. Jabez brings his request to God, and God grants it (4:9–10).

Work that matters. Craftsmen, linen workers and potters are named for their work (4:14, 21–23).

Simeon within Judah. Simeon’s towns lay inside Judah’s territory, which helps explain why their records stand together (4:24–33; Joshua 19:1–9).

Land and conflict. Simeon’s families expand by force. The Gedor expedition is dated to Hezekiah’s reign; the Seir expedition is undated. The record keeps the violence in view (4:38–43).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Jabez. His name sounds like the Hebrew word for pain, which gives his request about pain its force (4:9–10).

“Enlarge my territory.” A concrete request for land among Israel’s families (4:10). Applying it to wider responsibility or service is an application, not the original meaning of the words.

Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh. The wife of Mered, named among Judah’s families (4:18). The wording of 4:17–18 is difficult, and the text tells us nothing more about her.

Ge Harashim. A place whose name refers to craftsmen, as the note “for they were craftsmen” explains (4:14).

Meunites and Amalekites. Peoples displaced or defeated by Simeon’s families (4:41–43). The Amalekites had long been Israel’s enemies (1 Samuel 15).

“To this day.” The writer’s way of describing conditions in his own time (4:41, 43). It does not mean the same families live there now.

outline: 1 Chronicles 4:11–23 — Clans, Craftsmen, and Potters of Judah

sections.title: Clans, Craftsmen, and Potters of Judah

1.brief: The sons of Judah are listed as Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal. These names span several generations rather than one set of brothers, introducing Judah’s wider families beyond the royal line.
1.explain:
“The sons of Judah were Perez, Hezron, Carmi, Hur, and Shobal.”

After the royal genealogy of chapter 3, the record returns to Judah's other families. The heading “The sons of Judah” introduces names that span several generations rather than one set of brothers. “Perez” was Judah's son (2:4), “Hezron” was Perez's son (2:5), “Hur” was a descendant of Hezron through Caleb (2:19), and “Shobal” was Hur's son (2:50). The list therefore traces a line of descent within Judah, using “sons” in the broad sense of descendants. “Carmi” is unexpected here, since the Carmi of 2:7 belonged to Zerah's line. Many interpreters think the name stands for Caleb (Chelubai), Hur's father, which would make the list a straight line from Perez to Shobal. Either way, the verse introduces Judah's wider families beyond the royal household. After giving the line of kings its place, Chronicles turns to the ordinary households of the tribe.
1.notes:
The Hebrew name Carmi (karmi) and Chelubai (kelubai, 2:9) share some letters, and a copying change is possible.

Another possibility is that Carmi represents a different clan here. Translations generally retain “Carmi,” and the question remains open.

Joshua 7:1 gives Carmi's own descent in full: “Achan the son of Carmi, the son of Zabdi, the son of Zerah.”

2.brief: Reaiah the son of Shobal fathered Jahath, and Jahath fathered Ahumai and Lahad, the families of the Zorathites. The record links named ancestors with a clan known by its place of settlement.
2.explain:
“And Reaiah the son of Shobal begot Jahath,”

The genealogy follows “Shobal,” the last name in verse 1. His son “Reaiah” is probably the same as Haroeh, named among Shobal's descendants in 2:52. Reaiah fathered “Jahath.”

“and Jahath begot Ahumai and Lahad.”

Jahath's two sons were “Ahumai” and “Lahad.” Neither is mentioned elsewhere.

“These were the families of the Zorathites.”

These families made up “the Zorathites,” the people of Zorah, a town in the lowland of Judah (2:53). Chronicles links named ancestors with a clan known by its place of settlement. Zorah was the hometown of Samson's father Manoah (Judges 13:2), though Samson belonged to the tribe of Dan. These lists also associate families of Judah with Zorah.
2.notes:
Chapter 2:53 says that the Zorathites came from the families of Kirjath Jearim, descended from Shobal. This verse gives more detail about the same branch.

Chronicles often returns to a family to add information, which suggests that the genealogies draw on more than one source or record.

3.brief: The sons of the father of Etam are Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash, and their sister is named Hazelelponi. A daughter is remembered by name alongside her brothers.
3.explain:
“These were the sons of the father of Etam:”

The list names the family of “the father of Etam.” Etam was a town near Bethlehem, later fortified by Rehoboam (2 Chronicles 11:6). As elsewhere, “the father of” a town likely means its founding or leading ancestor.

“Jezreel, Ishma, and Idbash;”

Three sons are named. “Jezreel” is also the name of a town in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:56), the hometown of David's wife Ahinoam (3:1). “Ishma” and “Idbash” are otherwise unknown.

“and the name of their sister was Hazelelponi;”

The verse adds a sister, “Hazelelponi.” A daughter is remembered by name alongside her brothers. Her name is unusual and its meaning uncertain. Chronicles consistently includes women in its genealogies, and here a daughter whose life is otherwise unknown is given her own place.
3.notes: The Hebrew reads literally ‘These were the father of Etam,’ which is awkward. The Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, reads ‘the sons of Etam.’ The NKJV supplies “the sons of the father of Etam.” The exact relationship is uncertain, but the names clearly belong to a family associated with Etam.

4.brief: Penuel was the father of Gedor and Ezer the father of Hushah, and these are identified as sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah the father of Bethlehem. The verse ties these families and towns to Hur’s line and to Bethlehem.
4.explain:
“and Penuel was the father of Gedor, and Ezer was the father of Hushah.”

Two more family heads are named with their towns. “Penuel” was “the father of Gedor,” a town in the hill country of Judah (Joshua 15:58). “Ezer” was “the father of Hushah.” One of David's mighty men was “Sibbechai the Hushathite” (1 Chronicles 11:29), apparently from this town.

“These were the sons of Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah the father of Bethlehem.”

The verse identifies these families as descendants of “Hur, the firstborn of Ephrathah.” Hur was Caleb's son by Ephrath (2:19, 50). He is called “the father of Bethlehem,” connecting him with the town of David's birth. In 2:51 his son Salma is called the father of Bethlehem; here the title is given to Hur, the ancestor of the whole family. The verse ties these families and towns to Hur's line and to Bethlehem.

5.brief: Ashhur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah. The record introduces Ashhur’s household before naming the children of each wife.
5.explain:
“And Ashhur the father of Tekoa had two wives, Helah and Naarah.”

The record returns to “Ashhur the father of Tekoa,” the son born to Hezron after his death (2:24). Ashhur had “two wives, Helah and Naarah.” The genealogy introduces his household before naming the children of each wife. Tekoa, the town Ashhur's family founded or led, lay in the hill country south of Bethlehem. It later produced a wise woman (2 Samuel 14:2) and the prophet Amos (Amos 1:1). Chronicles remembers Tekoa's ancestral family by name.

6.brief: Naarah bore Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari. The children of Ashhur’s second-named wife are listed first.
6.explain:
“Naarah bore him Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni, and Haahashtari.”

The children of “Naarah,” Ashhur's second-named wife, are listed first. Her four sons were “Ahuzzam, Hepher, Temeni,” and “Haahashtari.” “Temeni” may mean ‘southerner,’ and “Haahashtari” appears to be a clan name, ‘the Ahashtarite.’ These names may represent clans as well as individuals.

“These were the sons of Naarah.”

The summary closes the list of Naarah's sons. Chronicles keeps each wife's children distinct, preserving the structure of the household. The reason Naarah's children are listed before Helah's is not given.
6.notes: The Hebrew form ha'ahashtari has a prefix meaning “the” and an ending that identifies membership in a people or clan. It follows the same pattern as “the Garmite” and “the Maachathite” in 4:19.

7.brief: Helah’s sons are Zereth, Zohar, and Ethnan. The other branch of Ashhur’s family is now recorded.
7.explain:
“The sons of Helah were Zereth, Zohar, and Ethnan;”

The other branch of Ashhur's family is now recorded. “Helah,” named first in verse 5, had three sons: “Zereth, Zohar,” and “Ethnan.” None of them is mentioned elsewhere. The list treats Ashhur's two families in turn, giving each its place. In a household with two wives, the children of both were remembered as part of the father's family.
7.notes: The written Hebrew text reads “Izhar” for the second name, while the traditional reading marked for pronunciation is “Zohar.” The NKJV follows the traditional reading.

8.brief: Koz fathered Anub, Zobebah, and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum. The list adds further families whose connection to the preceding names is not explained.
8.explain:
“and Koz begot Anub, Zobebah,”

The list continues with “Koz,” who fathered “Anub” and “Zobebah.” The connection of Koz to the preceding names is not explained. He may have been a son of Helah or of Ashhur, but the text does not say.

“and the families of Aharhel the son of Harum.”

Koz is also linked with “the families of Aharhel the son of Harum.” These families were evidently a recognized clan in Judah. The list adds further families whose connection to the preceding names is not explained. The compressed nature of these records sometimes leaves gaps, but each family has its place in Judah's history.
8.notes:
A priestly family called “the sons of Koz” appears among those who returned from exile (Ezra 2:61). That Koz belonged to a priestly line and is not the same as the Koz of this verse in Judah's genealogy.

1 Chronicles 4:9–10 — The Prayer of Jabez

9.brief: Jabez is introduced as more honorable than his brothers, and his mother named him Jabez, saying she bore him in pain. His name tied his birth to pain, which gives special force to the prayer that follows.
9.explain:
“Now Jabez was more honorable than his brothers,”

Suddenly the list of names pauses for a man named “Jabez.” His family relationship is not given. He is introduced with a verdict: he “was more honorable than his brothers.” The word “honorable” comes from the root associated with weight, glory, and honor. Jabez was respected, a man of weight and good standing among his family. The text does not say how he earned that honor. It is not a description of wealth or power. It is a description of character and standing, set before the prayer that follows.

“and his mother called his name Jabez, saying, ‘Because I bore him in pain.’”

His name came from his birth. His mother named him “Jabez,” saying, “Because I bore him in pain.” The name sounds like the Hebrew word for ‘pain,’ with letters rearranged. Every time someone called him by name, they recalled the pain of his birth. Names in Israel were often thought to say something about a person. A name tied to pain might have seemed to mark Jabez for sorrow. The mother's statement recalls the word spoken to Eve: “In pain you shall bring forth children” (Genesis 3:16). The pain of childbirth was part of life in a fallen world. Jabez's name carried that reminder.

His name tied his birth to pain, which gives special force to the prayer that follows. The man whose name meant pain asked God to keep him from pain.
9.notes:
The Hebrew name Jabez (ya'betz) and the Hebrew word for pain ('otzev) are closely related: the name uses the consonants of 'otzev with the last two reversed. The mother's explanation, “I bore him in pain” (be'otzev), uses the noun itself.

The International Standard Bible Encyclopedia explains the wordplay by reading the name as if it stood for the Hebrew expression ya'tzev, ‘he causes pain.’

Genesis 3:16, “In pain you shall bring forth children,” uses a related Hebrew noun from the same root, 'etsev, rather than 'otzev.

“More honorable” translates the Hebrew word nikbad, from kabed, ‘to be heavy’ or ‘to be honored.’ Here it describes someone held in high regard.

A town named Jabez appears in 2:55 as the home of scribal families. The text does not connect the man and the town, and Keil and Delitzsch leave open whether this Jabez was the town's founding ‘father.’

10.brief: Jabez calls on the God of Israel to bless him indeed, enlarge his territory, keep His hand with him, and keep him from evil so that he may not cause pain, and God grants what he requested. His dependent prayer is directed to God Himself, and the answer reported here is not a formula promising the same outcome to everyone who repeats his words.
10.explain:
“And Jabez called on the God of Israel saying,”

Jabez turned to God. He “called on the God of Israel,” the God of his fathers, the God who had made promises to Israel and given them their land. His prayer is directed to God Himself, not to a technique or a formula. The phrase “called on” describes earnest prayer, crying out to God for help.

“Oh, that You would bless me indeed,”

His first request was for God's blessing. “Bless me indeed” is emphatic: he asked God to bless him truly and fully. In the Old Testament, God's blessing included life, fruitfulness, provision, and His favor (Numbers 6:24–26). Jabez did not ask for blessing in general terms. He asked for God's blessing on his own life.

“and enlarge my territory,”

His second request was for land. “Territory” refers to the boundaries of his property, the land his family held. In Israel, land was the inheritance God had given to each tribe and family, and it provided for the family's life and future. Jabez asked God to enlarge it. The request had a concrete setting among Israel's families and lands. It was not a request for influence or ministry in a modern sense, though later readers may apply it by analogy to the responsibilities God entrusts to them.

“that Your hand would be with me,”

His third request was for God's presence and power. “Your hand” speaks of God's active help, guidance, and protection. Ezra later testified that the king granted his requests “according to the hand of the LORD his God upon him” (Ezra 7:6). Jabez wanted more than land. He wanted God's hand with him in whatever he received.

“and that You would keep me from evil, that I may not cause pain!”

His fourth request was for protection. “Keep me from evil” asks God to guard him from harm, trouble, or wrongdoing. “That I may not cause pain” echoes his name. The man named for pain asked God to keep him from pain, whether the pain of harm that might come to him or the pain he might cause others. His prayer reached beyond his name and the circumstances of his birth to the God who could change them.

“So God granted him what he requested.”

The account ends with God's answer. “God granted him what he requested.” The verse does not say how soon the answer came or how it was given. It simply reports that God heard and answered. A man whose name was associated with pain sought the God of Israel, and God granted his request.

The prayer of Jabez shows dependent prayer directed to God for blessing, provision, His accompanying hand, and protection. The answer reported here is not a formula promising the same outcome to everyone who repeats his words. Scripture teaches believers to ask according to God's will (1 John 5:14) and to pray, as Jesus did, “not My will, but Yours, be done” (Luke 22:42). What Jabez models is not a phrase to repeat but a heart that turned to God.
10.notes:
The prayer opens with the Hebrew particle 'im, usually ‘if.’ Here it expresses a strong wish, which the NKJV renders “Oh, that”; Gesenius lists this verse among places where 'im introduces a wish. The KJV margin gives the literal form, ‘If thou wilt.’

An alternative reading takes the prayer as a vow whose conclusion is left unstated, like Jacob's vow, “If God will be with me” (Genesis 28:20), but without the promise that follows there. Keil and Delitzsch, following Bertheau, read the verse this way.

The last clause is rendered “that I may not cause pain” (NKJV), ‘so that it might not bring me pain’ (ESV), and ‘so that I will be free from pain’ (NIV). The Hebrew wording ('otzbi) includes ‘me’ but does not state who causes the pain.

1 Chronicles 4:11–23 — Clans, Craftsmen, and Potters of Judah

11.brief: Chelub the brother of Shuhah fathered Mehir, who was the father of Eshton. The genealogy resumes after the account of Jabez.
11.explain:
“Chelub the brother of Shuhah begot Mehir,”

After the account of Jabez, the genealogy resumes. “Chelub” is a form of the name Caleb (compare Chelubai in 2:9), but this Chelub is identified as “the brother of Shuhah,” which distinguishes him from the other Calebs in the genealogies. He fathered “Mehir.”

“who was the father of Eshton.”

Mehir was “the father of Eshton.” These particular family relationships are not described elsewhere. The record returns to the rhythm of the lists, preserving family lines whose stories are not told.

12.brief: Eshton fathered Beth-Rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Ir-Nahash, and these are called the men of Rechah. Family names and place names again appear together.
12.explain:
“And Eshton begot Beth-Rapha, Paseah, and Tehinnah the father of Ir-Nahash.”

“Eshton” fathered three sons. “Beth-Rapha” is a place name, meaning ‘house of Rapha.’ “Paseah” is a personal name. “Tehinnah” was “the father of Ir-Nahash,” a town whose name means ‘city of the serpent’ or possibly ‘city of copper.’ Family names and place names again appear together.

“These were the men of Rechah.”

These families are called “the men of Rechah,” an otherwise unknown place or clan. The genealogy identifies them by their settlement. The genealogy's interest in places reflects the community's need to know where families belonged in the land.
12.notes:
The Encyclopaedia Judaica suggests that the town was originally called ‘Copper City’ (Ir Nehoshet), since the Hebrew word nahash (‘serpent’) resembles the Hebrew word nehoshet (‘copper, bronze’). The proposal is not confirmed, and the site of Ir-Nahash is uncertain.

Keil and Delitzsch take Nahash here as a personal name rather than the name of a town.

Some manuscripts of the ancient Greek translation known as the Septuagint, including Codex Vaticanus, read ‘Rechab’ instead of “Rechah,” which would connect these families with the Rechabites (2:55); others (Codex Alexandrinus) read ‘Repha.’ The Hebrew reading is retained in the NKJV.

13.brief: The sons of Kenaz are Othniel and Seraiah, and the list of Othniel’s sons begins with Hathath. Othniel, Israel’s first judge (Judges 3:9–11), is remembered here within Judah’s families.
13.explain:
“The sons of Kenaz were Othniel and Seraiah.”

Chronicles names “the sons of Kenaz.” “Othniel” was Israel's first judge. Joshua and Judges call him “Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother” (Judges 3:9). He captured Kirjath Sepher and received Caleb's daughter Achsah as his wife (Joshua 15:16–17). When Israel fell into idolatry and was oppressed by Cushan-Rishathaim, “The Spirit of the LORD came upon him, and he judged Israel,” and the land had rest for forty years (Judges 3:10–11). His brother “Seraiah” is otherwise unknown.

“The sons of Othniel were Hathath,”

The list of Othniel's sons begins with “Hathath,” who is otherwise unknown. Othniel, a deliverer raised up by God, is remembered here within Judah's families. His place in the genealogy honors a man through whom God rescued His people.
13.notes: The relationship between Kenaz and Caleb is debated. “Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother” (Judges 3:9) may mean that Othniel was Caleb's younger brother or that Kenaz was. Caleb's family is also called Kenizzite (Numbers 32:12; Joshua 14:14), which links them with Kenaz. The name Kenaz appears again in 4:15 as Caleb's grandson.

14.brief: The list of Othniel’s sons continues with Meonothai, who fathered Ophrah; Seraiah fathered Joab the father of Ge Harashim, the Valley of Craftsmen, so named because they were craftsmen. Skilled work is remembered as part of the community’s history.
14.explain:
“and Meonothai who begot Ophrah.”

The list of Othniel's sons continues with “Meonothai,” who fathered “Ophrah.” This Ophrah is a person, not the town of Gideon (Judges 6:11).

“Seraiah begot Joab the father of Ge Harashim,”

Othniel's brother “Seraiah” fathered “Joab,” who was “the father of Ge Harashim.” This Joab is unrelated to David's commander. “Ge Harashim” means ‘Valley of Craftsmen.’ A place called the Valley of Craftsmen is mentioned among the towns resettled after the exile (Nehemiah 11:35).

“for they were craftsmen.”

The note explains the name: “they were craftsmen.” The family of Joab gave their name to the valley where they practiced their skill. Skilled work is remembered as part of the community's history. Chronicles honors those who worked with their hands alongside judges and kings.
14.notes:
The Hebrew word harash refers to a skilled worker in wood, stone, or metal.

The same word is used for the workers in stone and timber David gathered for the temple (1 Chronicles 22:15).

15.brief: The sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh are Iru, Elah, and Naam, and Elah’s son is Kenaz. This is the faithful Caleb of Numbers 13–14, distinct from Caleb the son of Hezron in chapter 2.
15.explain:
“The sons of Caleb the son of Jephunneh were Iru, Elah, and Naam.”

The list names the family of “Caleb the son of Jephunneh.” This is the faithful Caleb of Numbers 13–14, one of the twelve spies sent into Canaan. When ten spies brought a fearful report, Caleb said, “Let us go up at once and take possession, for we are well able to overcome it” (Numbers 13:30). God said of him, “My servant Caleb, because he has a different spirit in him and has followed Me fully, I will bring into the land where he went” (Numbers 14:24). At eighty-five, Caleb received Hebron as his inheritance “because he wholly followed the LORD God of Israel” (Joshua 14:14). He is distinct from Caleb the son of Hezron in chapter 2. His sons were “Iru, Elah,” and “Naam.”

“The son of Elah was Kenaz.”

Caleb's grandson “Kenaz” shares a name with the ancestor of the Kenizzites. The record remembers Caleb's family briefly, but readers who knew his story would recall the man who followed the LORD fully.
15.notes:
The Hebrew reads literally ‘and the sons of Elah, and Kenaz,’ which may indicate that a name has been lost after “Elah.” The NKJV reads “The son of Elah was Kenaz.”

Achsah is named as Caleb's daughter both in 2:49, at the end of the family of Caleb the brother of Jerahmeel (2:42), and in Joshua 15:16, where her father is Caleb the son of Jephunneh (Joshua 15:13). The genealogies record both without explaining the relationship.

16.brief: The sons of Jehallelel are Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel. Another family is added to Judah’s record without further explanation of its connection.
16.explain:
“The sons of Jehallelel were Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria, and Asarel.”

The genealogy names the sons of “Jehallelel,” whose connection to the surrounding families is not explained. His four sons were “Ziph, Ziphah, Tiria,” and “Asarel.” “Ziph” is also the name of a town in the hill country of Judah (compare 2:42), near which David hid from Saul (1 Samuel 23:14). Another family is added to Judah's record without further explanation of its connection. The name Jehallelel means ‘he praises God.’

17.brief: The sons of Ezrah are Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon, and Mered’s wife bore Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa. The wording and arrangement of this verse and the next are difficult, and translations differ in how they assign the children.
17.explain:
“The sons of Ezrah were Jether, Mered, Epher, and Jalon.”

Chronicles names the sons of “Ezrah.” This Ezrah should not be identified with Ezra the scribe on the basis of the shared name. His four sons were “Jether, Mered, Epher,” and “Jalon.” “Mered” is the most important for what follows, because his wives and children are described in this verse and the next.

“And Mered's wife bore Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah the father of Eshtemoa.”

The NKJV supplies “Mered's wife” as the mother of “Miriam, Shammai,” and “Ishbah.” “Miriam” here may be a son or a daughter; the name is the same as that of Moses' sister. “Ishbah” was “the father of Eshtemoa,” a town in the hill country of Judah that later became a Levitical city (Joshua 21:14) and received gifts from David (1 Samuel 30:28). The wording and arrangement of this verse and the next are difficult, and translations differ in how they assign the children.
17.notes:
The Hebrew reads literally ‘and she conceived Miriam,’ without naming the mother.

This Miriam, a child of Mered's household, is a different person from Moses' sister, whose parents were Amram and Jochebed (Numbers 26:59).

Keil and Delitzsch report Bertheau's conjecture that the last sentence of verse 18, “these were the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took,” originally stood in verse 17 after Jalon, and the ESV and NASB print it there. On that arrangement Bithiah is the mother of Miriam, Shammai, and Ishbah, and Jehudijah's sons are Jered, Heber, and Jekuthiel. The rearrangement is a proposal and not the order of the Hebrew text.

18.brief: A parenthesis names the sons of Mered’s wife Jehudijah, the fathers of Gedor, Sochoh, and Zanoah, and the verse identifies other children as sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered married. An Egyptian princess is remembered within Judah’s families, though the text tells nothing more about her.
18.explain:
“(His wife Jehudijah bore Jered the father of Gedor, Heber the father of Sochoh, and Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah.)”

A parenthesis names the sons of Mered's other wife, “Jehudijah.” Her name means ‘the Judahite woman,’ distinguishing her from Mered's Egyptian wife. Her three sons were fathers of towns: “Jered the father of Gedor,” “Heber the father of Sochoh,” and “Jekuthiel the father of Zanoah.” Sochoh was where the Philistines camped before Goliath challenged Israel (1 Samuel 17:1). Zanoah was a town in Judah's lowland (Joshua 15:34).

“And these were the sons of Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took.”

The verse identifies other children as sons of “Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh, whom Mered took” as his wife. An Egyptian princess is remembered within Judah's families, though the text tells nothing more about her. Her name means ‘daughter of the LORD,’ which may suggest that she had embraced Israel's God, though that is an inference from the name rather than a statement of the text. Her marriage to Mered shows once again that Judah's family record included people from other nations.
18.notes: The text does not identify Bithiah with the unnamed daughter of Pharaoh who rescued Moses (Exodus 2:5–10), and it gives no date for Mered or Bithiah.

19.brief: The sons of Hodiah’s wife, the sister of Naham, are named as the fathers of Keilah the Garmite and of Eshtemoa the Maachathite. The record again connects family lines with towns of Judah.
19.explain:
“The sons of Hodiah's wife, the sister of Naham,”

The list names the sons of “Hodiah's wife,” who is described as “the sister of Naham.” The Hebrew is unclear; Hodiah may be the husband or the wife's own name. Her family is remembered through her children.

“were the fathers of Keilah the Garmite and of Eshtemoa the Maachathite.”

Her sons were “the fathers of Keilah the Garmite and of Eshtemoa the Maachathite.” Keilah was a town in Judah's lowland that David rescued from the Philistines (1 Samuel 23:1–5). “The Garmite” and “the Maachathite” describe clans associated with these towns. The record again connects family lines with towns of Judah.
19.notes:
The KJV reads ‘the sons of his wife Hodiah,’ making Hodiah the wife's name. The Hebrew expression 'eshet means ‘wife of’ and connects the woman to the name that follows. Keil and Delitzsch understand this to mean that Hodiah is the husband, as in the NKJV and ESV.

Elsewhere the Maachathites were the people of Maacah, a small Aramean kingdom named with Geshur in the region of Mount Hermon and Bashan (Joshua 13:11; “Syrian Maacah,” 1 Chronicles 19:6).

Keil and Delitzsch suggest instead that the Maachathite of Eshtemoa descended from Caleb through his concubine Maachah (2:48). The text does not explain the term.

20.brief: Shimon’s sons are Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-Hanan, and Tilon, and Ishi’s sons are Zoheth and Ben-Zoheth. These households extend Judah’s family record, although their connection to the preceding families is not supplied.
20.explain:
“And the sons of Shimon were Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-Hanan, and Tilon.”

The genealogy names the sons of “Shimon.” His four sons were “Amnon, Rinnah, Ben-Hanan,” and “Tilon.” This Amnon is unrelated to David's son (3:1).

“And the sons of Ishi were Zoheth and Ben-Zoheth.”

The sons of “Ishi” were “Zoheth” and “Ben-Zoheth.” The name Ben-Zoheth means ‘son of Zoheth,’ which may indicate a grandson rather than a second son. These households extend Judah's family record, although their connection to the preceding families is not supplied. This Ishi is distinct from Ishi the son of Appaim (2:31) and Ishi of Simeon (4:42).

21.brief: The sons of Shelah the son of Judah include Er the father of Lecah and Laadah the father of Mareshah, along with the families of the house of the linen workers of the house of Ashbea. The line of Judah’s third son is remembered partly through a skilled trade.
21.explain:
“The sons of Shelah the son of Judah were”

Chronicles turns to the line of “Shelah,” Judah's third son by the daughter of Shua (2:3). Shelah was the son Judah withheld from Tamar (Genesis 38:11, 26). His family is recorded here.

“Er the father of Lecah, Laadah the father of Mareshah,”

Shelah's son “Er” bore the name of Shelah's older brother who died (2:3). He was “the father of Lecah,” an otherwise unknown place. “Laadah” was “the father of Mareshah,” a town in Judah's lowland where King Asa later defeated Zerah the Ethiopian (2 Chronicles 14:9–12).

“and the families of the house of the linen workers of the house of Ashbea;”

Shelah's line also included “the families of the house of the linen workers.” These were skilled workers in fine linen, a valued fabric used for priestly garments and the clothing of the wealthy. They belonged to “the house of Ashbea,” perhaps a guild or clan workshop. The line of Judah's third son is remembered partly through a skilled trade.
21.notes: The Hebrew word butz refers to fine linen, a high-quality fabric. Chronicles uses it for the robes worn by David, the Levites who carried the ark, and the singers (1 Chronicles 15:27; compare 2 Chronicles 5:12) and the materials of the temple (2 Chronicles 2:14; 3:14).

22.brief: The list continues with Jokim, the men of Chozeba, Joash, Saraph who ruled in Moab, and Jashubi-Lehem. The closing note identifies these records as ancient.
22.explain:
“also Jokim, the men of Chozeba, and Joash;”

The list of Shelah's descendants continues with “Jokim,” “the men of Chozeba,” and “Joash.” “Chozeba” is probably the same as Chezib, where Shelah was born (Genesis 38:5). The men of Chozeba were Shelah's descendants who lived there.

“Saraph, who ruled in Moab, and Jashubi-Lehem.”

“Saraph” is said to have “ruled in Moab,” an unusual notice of a Judahite family with authority or holdings in Moab, east of the Dead Sea. “Jashubi-Lehem” is otherwise unknown.

“Now the records are ancient.”

The closing note says that “the records are ancient.” The writer of Chronicles was working with old sources that came from Israel's distant past. This note shows the care with which the genealogies were compiled. The writer did not invent these names; he received and preserved them.
22.notes:
The phrase “who ruled in Moab” can also be translated ‘who married into Moab.’ The Hebrew verb ba'al can mean to rule or to marry. Either reading shows a connection between Shelah's family and Moab.

Jerome's Latin translation reads Jashubi-Lehem as a description, ‘who returned to Lahem,’ and the ESV similarly has ‘returned to Lehem.’ Lehem may be Bethlehem. The Hebrew is uncertain.

The Hebrew reads literally ‘and the words are ancient’; the noun devarim can also mean ‘matters’ or ‘things’ (KJV ‘these are ancient things’).

23.brief: These were the potters who lived at Netaim and Gederah, where they dwelt with the king for his work. Ordinary skilled labor in royal service is honored within the record of God’s people.
23.explain:
“These were the potters”

The list identifies some of Shelah's descendants as “potters.” Pottery was essential in the ancient world, used for storage, cooking, and trade. Skilled potters were valued workers.

“and those who dwell at Netaim and Gederah;”

They lived at “Netaim” and “Gederah.” The names mean ‘plantations’ and ‘walls’ or ‘sheepfolds.’ Gederah was a town in Judah's lowland (Joshua 15:36).

“there they dwelt with the king for his work.”

The potters lived “with the king for his work.” They were employed in royal service, producing pottery for the king's needs. The text does not say which king or what work they did. Ordinary skilled labor in royal service is honored within the record of God's people. The chapter that includes the prayer of Jabez also remembers potters at their wheels.
23.notes:
Archaeologists have found many storage jar handles in Judah stamped with the Hebrew word lamelekh (‘belonging to the king’), dating to the late eighth century BC and widely associated with Hezekiah's reign (some scholars place the start of the system slightly earlier). The jars belonged to a royal administrative system. They illustrate the kind of royal pottery production this verse describes, though the verse itself does not identify a period.

1 Chronicles 4:24–33 — Simeon’s Families and Towns

24.brief: The record turns to Simeon, naming his sons Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul. Simeon follows Judah because its towns lay within Judah’s territory (Joshua 19:1–9).
24.explain:
“The sons of Simeon were Nemuel, Jamin, Jarib, Zerah, and Shaul,”

The record now turns to the tribe of “Simeon,” Jacob's second son. Simeon follows Judah because its towns lay within Judah's territory: “their inheritance was within the inheritance of the children of Judah” (Joshua 19:1). Simeon's five sons are named. “Shaul” is called in Genesis “the son of a Canaanite woman” (Genesis 46:10). Simeon remains a named tribe with its own family history, even though its land was within Judah's.
24.notes:
Genesis 46:10 and Exodus 6:15 list six sons of Simeon: Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jachin, Zohar, and Shaul. Numbers 26:12–13 lists five, as here, omitting Ohad, perhaps because his line did not continue. “Nemuel” corresponds to Jemuel, “Jarib” to Jachin, and “Zerah” to Zohar. These are variant forms.

Joshua 19:9 gives the reason Simeon's inheritance was taken from Judah's portion: “for the share of the children of Judah was too much for them.”

25.brief: Shallum, Mibsam, and Mishma continue Simeon’s line, each the son of the one before. The record traces one branch of Simeon through successive generations.
25.explain:
“Shallum his son, Mibsam his son, and Mishma his son.”

The genealogy traces one branch of Simeon through successive generations. “Shallum” was apparently Shaul's son, and he was followed by “Mibsam” and “Mishma,” each the son of the one before. The names “Mibsam” and “Mishma” also appear among the sons of Ishmael (1:29–30). The repetition of names may suggest connections between the tribe of Simeon and Ishmaelite or Arabian peoples in the southern regions, though the text does not say so.

26.brief: Mishma’s descendants are Hamuel, Zacchur, and Shimei, again in a father-to-son sequence. The line reaches Shimei, whose family is described next.
26.explain:
“And the sons of Mishma were Hamuel his son, Zacchur his son, and Shimei his son.”

Mishma's descendants continue the father-to-son sequence. “Hamuel,” “Zacchur,” and “Shimei” each follow in turn. The line reaches “Shimei,” whose family is described in the next verse. Chronicles traces Simeon's line through six generations from Shaul, focusing on the branch that would become most numerous.

27.brief: Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters, but his brothers had few children, and none of Simeon’s families multiplied as much as the children of Judah. The record notes Simeon’s smaller growth without presenting it as a judgment on the tribe’s worth.
27.explain:
“Shimei had sixteen sons and six daughters;”

“Shimei” had a large family: “sixteen sons and six daughters.” His family stood out within Simeon.

“but his brothers did not have many children,”

In contrast, Shimei's “brothers did not have many children.” His family was the exception.

“nor did any of their families multiply as much as the children of Judah.”

The list compares Simeon's growth with Judah's. “Nor did any of their families multiply as much as the children of Judah.” Simeon remained a small tribe. In the wilderness census its numbers fell sharply, from 59,300 in the first count (Numbers 1:23) to 22,200 in the second (Numbers 26:14). The record notes Simeon's smaller growth without presenting it as a judgment on the tribe's worth. Smaller numbers do not prove lesser spiritual standing, and the text supplies no reason for the difference.
27.notes: Simeon is not mentioned in Moses's blessing of the tribes in Deuteronomy 33. The reason is not stated.

28.brief: Simeon’s people dwelt at Beersheba, Moladah, and Hazar Shual. The list of their towns begins with places in the southern region of the land.
28.explain:
“They dwelt at Beersheba, Moladah, Hazar Shual,”

The list of Simeon's towns begins with places in the southern region of the land, the Negev. “Beersheba” was the most famous, the place where Abraham and Isaac dug wells and called on the LORD (Genesis 21:33; 26:23–25), and the traditional southern limit of Israel in the phrase “from Dan to Beersheba” (1 Samuel 3:20). “Moladah” and “Hazar Shual” were nearby towns. The list follows Joshua 19:2–3, the record of Simeon's allotment. Nehemiah 11:26–27 lists these towns among those resettled after the exile.
28.notes: Simeon's towns appear in Joshua 19:2–8 and also among Judah's southern towns in Joshua 15:26–32. The overlap reflects Simeon's location within Judah's territory.

29.brief: Bilhah, Ezem, and Tolad are added to Simeon’s towns. The record continues to preserve the places that made up the tribe’s dwelling.
29.explain:
“Bilhah, Ezem, Tolad,”

The list of Simeon's towns continues. “Bilhah,” “Ezem,” and “Tolad” were towns in the Negev. Joshua 19:3–4 lists them as Balah, Ezem, and Eltolad. The genealogy continues to preserve the places that made up the tribe's dwelling. For a community returning to the land, knowing where their ancestors had lived mattered.
29.notes: Joshua 19:3 reads “Balah” and 15:29 “Baalah” for Bilhah. Joshua 19:4 reads “Eltolad” for Tolad.

30.brief: Bethuel, Hormah, and Ziklag are named among Simeon’s towns. Ziklag later became significant in David’s story (1 Samuel 27:6).
30.explain:
“Bethuel, Hormah, Ziklag,”

Three more towns are named. “Bethuel” is called Bethul in Joshua 19:4. “Hormah” was the site of an early victory over the Canaanites in the wilderness period (Numbers 21:3). “Ziklag” later became significant in David's story. While David was fleeing from Saul, the Philistine king Achish gave him Ziklag, and the narrator adds, “Therefore Ziklag has belonged to the kings of Judah to this day” (1 Samuel 27:6). Ziklag was David's base until he became king in Hebron.

31.brief: Beth Marcaboth, Hazar Susim, Beth Biri, and Shaaraim complete the list, and these were Simeon’s cities until the reign of David. The note marks a change in their settlement by David’s time without explaining it.
31.explain:
“Beth Marcaboth, Hazar Susim, Beth Biri, and at Shaaraim.”

The list of cities is completed. “Beth Marcaboth” means ‘house of chariots’ and “Hazar Susim” ‘village of horses.’ These names may reflect later use as royal chariot stations, perhaps from Solomon's time, when he kept chariot cities (1 Kings 9:19). “Beth Biri” and “Shaaraim” complete the list.

“These were their cities until the reign of David.”

The note says that “these were their cities until the reign of David.” It marks a change in their settlement by David's time without explaining it. Perhaps these towns were absorbed into Judah's administration or the royal domain under David, as Ziklag was (1 Samuel 27:6). The note shows that Simeon's history continued to change over time.
31.notes: Joshua 19:5–6 reads “Hazar Susah,” “Beth Lebaoth,” and “Sharuhen” for Hazar Susim, Beth Biri, and Shaaraim.

32.brief: Their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan, five cities. Smaller settlements are recorded alongside the main cities.
32.explain:
“And their villages were Etam, Ain, Rimmon, Tochen, and Ashan—five cities—”

Smaller settlements are recorded alongside the main cities. “Etam” here is a different town from the Etam near Bethlehem (4:3). “Ain” and “Rimmon” may have been neighboring towns, later known together as En Rimmon (Nehemiah 11:29). “Ashan” later became a Levitical city (1 Chronicles 6:59). The total is “five cities.” Chronicles preserves the full extent of Simeon's dwelling places.
32.notes: Joshua 19:7 lists “Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan: four cities.” Chronicles adds Etam and has Tochen where Joshua has Ether. The differences may reflect changes in settlement or variations in the sources.

33.brief: All the villages around these cities as far as Baal were their dwelling places, and they kept their genealogy. The note emphasizes that Simeon preserved its family records and introduces the names that follow.
33.explain:
“and all the villages that were around these cities as far as Baal.”

Simeon's territory included “all the villages that were around these cities as far as Baal.” Joshua 19:8 identifies this as Baalath Beer, Ramah of the South. The description outlines the extent of Simeon's land.

“These were their dwelling places, and they maintained their genealogy:”

The verse concludes the list of towns and emphasizes that Simeon “maintained their genealogy.” They kept records of their families. The note introduces the list of leaders that follows. For the community after the exile, maintaining genealogies was essential for establishing identity, inheritance, and the right to serve (compare Ezra 2:62). Simeon's preserved records are part of what Chronicles honors.
33.notes:
The Hebrew reads literally ‘and their genealogical record was theirs,’ noting that Simeon had its own family records. Similar notices of genealogical records appear in 5:7, 17; 9:1, 22.

1 Chronicles 4:34–43 — Simeon’s Expansion

34.brief: The list of Simeon’s leaders begins with Meshobab, Jamlech, and Joshah the son of Amaziah. These are among the family heads whose actions the following verses describe.
34.explain:
“Meshobab, Jamlech, and Joshah the son of Amaziah;”

The list of Simeon's leaders begins. “Meshobab” and “Jamlech” are named alone, and “Joshah” is identified as “the son of Amaziah.” These are among the family heads whose actions the following verses describe. They led their families during a period of growth and expansion. Their names are preserved because they were leaders in their tribe.

35.brief: Joel is named, along with Jehu, whose ancestry is traced through Joshibiah, Seraiah, and Asiel. Fuller ancestry establishes the place of some leaders within the tribe.
35.explain:
“Joel, and Jehu the son of Joshibiah, the son of Seraiah, the son of Asiel;”

“Joel” is named, along with “Jehu,” whose ancestry is traced through “Joshibiah,” “Seraiah,” and “Asiel.” Fuller ancestry establishes the place of some leaders within the tribe. Tracing Jehu's family through three generations shows that his standing rested on recognized descent. This Jehu is unrelated to the king of Israel by that name.

36.brief: Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, and Benaiah are added to the list of leaders. The record names each of them individually.
36.explain:
“Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel, and Benaiah;”

Seven more leaders are named: “Elioenai, Jaakobah, Jeshohaiah, Asaiah, Adiel, Jesimiel,” and “Benaiah.” The list names each of them individually. “Jaakobah” is a form of the name Jacob. Several names include Hebrew elements referring to God (El) or the LORD (-iah), expressing faith in Israel's God. These men were part of the leadership that guided Simeon's families.

37.brief: Ziza is named with his ancestry traced through five generations back to Shemaiah. The list of Simeon’s leaders closes with this detailed lineage.
37.explain:
“Ziza the son of Shiphi, the son of Allon, the son of Jedaiah, the son of Shimri, the son of Shemaiah—”

The list of Simeon's leaders closes with “Ziza,” whose ancestry is traced through five generations back to “Shemaiah.” This is the most detailed lineage in the list. Ziza's standing as a leader rested on his recognized place in the family line. The careful tracing of generations shows how much Simeon valued its genealogical records (4:33).

38.brief: These men mentioned by name were leaders in their families, and their father’s house increased greatly. Their growth explains the search for land that follows.
38.explain:
“these mentioned by name were leaders in their families,”

The verse sums up the preceding list. “These mentioned by name were leaders in their families.” They were the heads of their households and clans.

“and their father's house increased greatly.”

Their families “increased greatly.” Though Simeon as a whole did not multiply as much as Judah (4:27), these families grew. Their growth explains the search for land that follows. The need for pasture for growing families and flocks drove them to seek new territory.

39.brief: They went to the entrance of Gedor, as far as the east side of the valley, to seek pasture for their flocks. The movement is driven by the practical needs of a growing shepherding people.
39.explain:
“So they went to the entrance of Gedor,”

The growing families went out in search of land. They traveled “to the entrance of Gedor.” The location is uncertain; it is probably a different place from the Gedor in Judah's hill country (4:4, 18).

“as far as the east side of the valley,”

They went “as far as the east side of the valley,” a region otherwise unidentified.

“to seek pasture for their flocks.”

Their purpose was practical: “to seek pasture for their flocks.” Simeon's people were shepherds, and their growing herds needed grazing land. The movement is driven by the practical needs of a growing shepherding people.
39.notes: The Septuagint, an ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament, reads ‘Gerar’ instead of “Gedor.” Gerar was a region in the western Negev between Gaza and Beersheba, where Abraham and Isaac had lived among the Philistines (Genesis 20:1; 26:1), and where Asa pursued the Cushites (2 Chronicles 14:13). The reference to Hamites in verse 40 would fit Gerar. Its exact site is debated. The NKJV follows the Hebrew reading.

40.brief: They found rich, good pasture in land that was broad, quiet, and peaceful, where some Hamites had formerly lived. The description explains why the region attracted them.
40.explain:
“And they found rich, good pasture,”

They found what they were looking for. The pasture was “rich” and “good,” ideal for their flocks.

“and the land was broad, quiet, and peaceful;”

The land was “broad, quiet, and peaceful.” It offered room for expansion and peaceful conditions. The verse does not describe the inhabitants’ military preparations. The description recalls the Danites' discovery of Laish, whose people were “quiet and secure” (Judges 18:7), before the Danites attacked them.

“for some Hamites formerly lived there.”

The inhabitants were “some Hamites,” descendants of Ham (1:8). These may have been Egyptians, Cushites, or Canaanites living in the region. The description explains why the region attracted Simeon's families: good land, peaceful conditions, and inhabitants who were not part of Israel.
40.notes: “Formerly lived there” renders a phrase that may mean the Hamites had lived there from of old, or that they had been living there up to that time. The latter is more likely, since the next verse describes the attack on the people found there.

41.brief: In the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, these men attacked the tents and the Meunites found there, utterly destroyed them, and settled in their place because of the pasture. The verse anchors this episode in Hezekiah’s reign and records the violence of the conquest plainly, without making it a pattern for God’s people today.
41.explain:
“These recorded by name came in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah;”

The verse anchors this episode in history. The leaders “recorded by name” in verses 34–37 came “in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah,” who reigned in the late eighth and early seventh centuries BC. The reference dates this particular episode. It does not date every genealogy in the chapter.

“and they attacked their tents and the Meunites who were found there,”

They attacked the inhabitants, who lived in “tents,” suggesting a semi-nomadic population, along with “the Meunites who were found there.” The Meunites were a people of the southern desert, against whom King Uzziah also fought (2 Chronicles 26:7).

“and utterly destroyed them, as it is to this day.”

They “utterly destroyed them.” The phrase describes total destruction, the same language used for the conquest of Canaan. The verse records the violence of the conquest plainly. “As it is to this day” speaks from the writer's historical standpoint.

“So they dwelt in their place, because there was pasture for their flocks there.”

The Simeonites settled in the land they had taken, “because there was pasture for their flocks there.” The verse records the violence plainly, without making it a pattern for God's people today. These reports do not authorize modern seizure of land, ethnic hostility, or violence in God's name.
41.notes:
“Utterly destroyed” translates the Hebrew verb haram, used for devoting something to destruction, especially in the conquest narratives (Joshua 6:21; 1 Samuel 15:3). The text does not say whether this action was commanded by God.

Hezekiah's reign is commonly dated about 715–686 BC, though some chronologies place it about a decade earlier.

42.brief: Five hundred men of Simeon, led by Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi, went to Mount Seir. A further expedition carries Simeon’s story into the region of Edom.
42.explain:
“Now some of them, five hundred men of the sons of Simeon, went to Mount Seir,”

A further expedition carries Simeon's story into the region of Edom. “Five hundred men of the sons of Simeon” went to “Mount Seir,” the mountainous region south of the Dead Sea associated with Esau and the Edomites (1:38).

“having as their captains Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah, and Uzziel, the sons of Ishi.”

The expedition was led by four brothers, “Pelatiah, Neariah, Rephaiah,” and “Uzziel, the sons of Ishi.” This Ishi is a Simeonite, distinct from Ishi of Judah (4:20). The leaders are named because they directed the campaign.
42.notes: The text does not say whether this expedition took place in Hezekiah's time or at another period. It may have been part of the same expansion described in verses 39–41.

43.brief: They defeated the rest of the Amalekites who had escaped and have dwelt there to the writer’s day. The chapter closes with Simeonites settled in that region, recalling Israel’s long conflict with Amalek (1 Samuel 15).
43.explain:
“And they defeated the rest of the Amalekites who had escaped.”

The Simeonites “defeated the rest of the Amalekites who had escaped.” The Amalekites were Israel's longstanding enemies, descendants of Esau's grandson Amalek (1:36). They attacked Israel in the wilderness, and God declared war on Amalek “from generation to generation” (Exodus 17:16). Saul fought them and failed to carry out God's judgment completely (1 Samuel 15:7–9). David also fought them, and some escaped (1 Samuel 30:17). These accounts provide background for the reference to surviving Amalekites, but Chronicles does not identify the particular conflict from which this group had escaped.

“They have dwelt there to this day.”

The Simeonites settled in the region of Seir and “have dwelt there to this day,” that is, up to the writer's own time. The chapter closes with Simeonites settled in that region, recalling Israel's long conflict with Amalek. The closing statement speaks from the writer's historical standpoint; it does not promise that the same families occupy those places today.
43.notes: Chronicles mentions Amalek once more, among the nations from whose spoil David dedicated silver and gold to the LORD (1 Chronicles 18:11).
